stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Scratch-resistant coatings are usually applied as liquids and then hardened with heat. In a recent trial, however, a research team pressed a dry film directly onto eyeglass lenses. The thin layer of silica particles that the team bonded to the ______ the lenses from visible wear for more than a year of daily use.
explanation: Cross out the clause in the middle ("that the team bonded to the plastic"). You are left with the subject "The thin layer of silica particles" and its verb "shielded." Nothing goes between a subject and its verb, even when the subject is long. This is the basic move behind every Boundaries question where a long subject tempts you to pause before the main verb.

B.why: You added a comma because the subject is long and you wanted to take a breath before the verb. A comma never separates a subject from its verb, however long the subject is.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "The thin layer of silica particles that the team bonded to the plastic" has no main verb, so it is a fragment, and "shielded the lenses..." has no subject.

D.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it. Everything before the colon is a subject still waiting for its verb, so you have cut the sentence's subject off from "shielded."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Sprint coaches have long debated whether the start or the top-speed phase of a race matters more. To test the question, physiologists fitted force sensors to the starting blocks and to a stretch of track. During each trial, they ______ the athletes' legs produced in the first ten meters.
explanation: Ask what the athletes' force was to the physiologists: it is what they measured. "How much force the athletes' legs produced" is the object of the verb "measured," and nothing goes between a verb and its object. You will need this on real Boundaries questions where a long "how" or "what" clause comes right after the verb.

B.why: You put a comma where the sentence felt like it should pause. A verb and its object belong together, so a comma here splits "measured" from what was measured.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides. "How much force the athletes' legs produced in the first ten meters" cannot stand on its own. It is the object of "measured."

D.why: The period leaves "How much force the athletes' legs produced in the first ten meters" as a fragment. It is not a question, and it has no main clause of its own.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Folklorists who study trickster tales often track a single story as it travels from village to village. In one survey of a mountain region, researchers recorded more than three hundred tales. The ______ the greatest number of local versions features a fox who outwits a miller by hiding inside a grain sack.
explanation: "That has the greatest number of local versions" tells you which tale you are talking about. Without it, "the one" could be any of the three hundred. A clause that identifies the noun is essential and takes no punctuation. This rule decides the real Boundaries questions where a choice slips a comma in front of "that."

B.why: You treated the "that" clause as extra information to set off. It is the information that picks out which tale you mean, so it cannot be set off. A comma here also sits between the subject "The one" and its verb "features."

C.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it, and "The one" is only the start of a subject. The colon also separates the noun from the clause that identifies it.

D.why: A single dash works like a colon, so the text before it would have to be a complete sentence. "The one" is not. A dash used to open an interruption would also need a matching dash to close it, and none appears.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Excavators working at a Bronze Age hillside settlement spent two full seasons mapping the floor of a single house. Before lifting any objects from the soil, they photographed and catalogued the bronze pins found near the ______ the clay beads scattered along the north wall.
explanation: "And" joins two parallel noun phrases, "the bronze pins found near the hearth" and "the clay beads scattered along the north wall." Both are objects of "catalogued." When "and" joins just two items that are not complete sentences, it takes no comma. You will use this on real Boundaries questions where two long, parallel phrases make a comma before "and" look natural.

B.why: You used the comma that goes before "and" when it joins two complete sentences. What follows "and" here is only a noun phrase with no verb of its own, so the comma does not belong.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "And the clay beads scattered along the north wall" is a phrase, not a sentence.

D.why: A colon announces something, such as a list, an example, or an explanation. Here it cuts the second object off from the verb "catalogued," and "and" directly after a colon has nothing to connect.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Public health officials track many numbers during a measles outbreak, but one matters more than the rest. The share of children in a community who have received both doses of the measles ______ whether the virus can keep moving from one household to the next.
explanation: Find the main verb first: it is "determines." Everything before it, from "The share" through "vaccine," is one long subject. A subject and its verb are never separated by punctuation, however long the subject is. So the blank needs no punctuation: "The share ... of the measles vaccine determines whether the virus can keep moving." This drill sets up the real Boundaries questions where a long subject runs up to the blank and the correct choice is the one with no punctuation.

A.why: You added a comma because the subject is long and you wanted to pause before the verb. Commas never come between a subject and its verb. Cross out the middle ("The share ... determines whether...") and you can see the comma cuts the sentence's main link in two. This is the trap these questions are built around.

B.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "The share of children ... of the measles vaccine" has no verb, so it is a fragment, and so is "determines whether the virus..." The semicolon splits one sentence into two fragments.

D.why: A colon must follow a complete sentence. The words before it are only a subject with no verb yet, so a colon has nothing to stand on. It also cuts the subject off from its verb, "determines."
